strengths: Introduces a large-scale (139,981 image) synthetic dataset for salient object detection generated via a novel multi-modal diffusion pipeline that fuses FLUX DiT intermediate features, concept attention maps, and DINO-v3 representations, avoiding reliance on a separate teacher segmentation model.

Iterative, feedback-driven generation strategy that reweights category sampling based on per-category model performance is a sensible and demonstrated-effective (Table 5) mechanism for continual dataset improvement.

Ambiguity-aware multi-mask decoder built on DPT + DINO-v3 is simple yet effective, and the paper provides an honest oracle-vs-non-oracle comparison (S3OD vs S3OD*) to illustrate the residual ambiguity gap.

Extensive experimental evaluation: cross-dataset generalization across six benchmarks, fine-tuned SOTA comparisons, comparisons to other synthetic-data methods (MaskFactory, DatasetDM) under matched data budgets, and multiple ablations (data modalities, iterative rounds, architecture/backbone, prompt engineering, model efficiency).

Reasonable quality-control pipeline (consistency filtering, VLM-based mask/semantic validation) and quantitative synthetic image quality metrics (IS, FID) benchmarked against prior synthetic SOD data generators.
Good coverage and organization of related work situating the contribution relative to pseudo-labeling, diffusion-based segmentation synthesis, and existing SOD architectures.
weaknesses: Reproducibility is unclear: no explicit statement about dataset/code release, generation pipeline hyperparameters (e.g., number of categories, held-out set size for the iterative feedback loop, LLM prompt count per round) are only partially specified.

Cross-dataset generalization comparisons (Table 2) pit S3OD (trained on 139K synthetic images) against baselines trained on much smaller real datasets (DIS, HRSOD-TR, etc.); while Table 4 partially controls for data volume, the headline generalization claims in the abstract/intro (20-50% error reduction) are not clearly disentangled from a pure data-scale effect versus the proposed multi-modal generation method itself.

The architectural contribution (multi-mask decoder with IoU-based branch selection) is a fairly direct application of existing multiple-choice-learning/ambiguity-modeling ideas (Guzman-Rivera et al., Rupprecht et al.) to SOD, limiting novelty on the modeling side; most novelty resides in the data pipeline.

Ablation in Table 6 shows relatively modest differences between using all three modalities versus DINO-v3+DiT alone on several benchmarks, raising questions about whether the added complexity (concept attention maps, fusion module) is fully justified.

Manual quality verification of the dataset is based on only 1,000 randomly sampled masks with no description of annotator qualifications, agreement statistics, or evaluation protocol, limiting confidence in the reported 98.5% quality rate.

No discussion of limitations, failure cases, potential biases inherited from the FLUX diffusion model (e.g., underrepresented object categories, cultural/visual biases), or societal/ethical considerations of relying on purely synthetic training data.

Minor writing/presentation issues (e.g., typos such as 'siginificantly', inconsistent capitalization of dataset name, dense notation in Section 3) reduce clarity and would benefit from another editing pass.
No error bars, variance across seeds, or statistical significance testing are reported for the main results, making it hard to assess whether reported improvements are robust.

strengths: Addresses an important and well-motivated problem: data scarcity for pixel-precise salient object detection annotations across the DIS and HR-SOD subtasks.

Technically interesting idea of extracting mask supervision directly from the generative process (FLUX DiT intermediate features + concept attention maps) combined with DINO-v3 features, avoiding reliance on an external frozen teacher segmentation model.

Large-scale dataset (139K images) is notably larger than existing SOD benchmarks combined, and the paper includes a reasonably broad set of ablations (modality contributions, iterative generation rounds, architecture/backbone choice, prompt generation strategy).

Evaluation spans six standard benchmarks (DIS-5K, HRSOD, UHRSD, DUTS, DUT-OMRON, DAVIS-S) with standard SOD metrics, and reports both zero-shot cross-dataset generalization and fine-tuned SOTA comparisons.
Reasonable model efficiency relative to competing high-resolution SOD architectures (Table 10).
weaknesses: No statement of dataset/code release; given the paper's central contribution is a large synthetic dataset and generation pipeline requiring substantial compute (8xH200, 2 days), reproducibility is a serious concern without concrete release commitments or details sufficient to replicate the pipeline (e.g., exact consistency-filtering model, exact FID/IS reference sets).

Key cross-dataset comparisons (Table 2, Table 3) pit a model trained on 139K+ synthetic images against baselines trained on only a few thousand real images; this scale confound is not properly isolated as the main result, making it hard to attribute gains to the proposed multi-modal label-extraction method versus simply using far more training data. Only the smaller controlled comparison in Table 4 (10K subsample) partially addresses this, and even there the comparison set of synthetic baselines is limited (only MaskFactory and DatasetDM).

The central 'ambiguity-aware' claim is not convincingly validated: SOD benchmarks used only have a single ground-truth mask per image, so the multi-mask head's value for genuine annotation ambiguity is never tested against real multi-annotator data; the oracle variant (S3OD*) uses ground truth to pick the best of three masks, which the authors admit is not comparable to other methods, undermining the claimed practical benefit of ambiguity modeling.

Benefit of the iterative generation framework appears marginal by the third round (e.g., DIS F-measure moves from .880 to .881 after adding 50K more images in Table 5), raising doubts about the scalability/necessity of the proposed feedback-driven weighting scheme relative to simply generating more diverse data upfront.

Important hyperparameters (e.g., α=8, β=0.5 in the category reweighting function, consistency threshold τ=0.8, filtering thresholds) are stated without ablation or sensitivity analysis, and the manual quality audit (1,000 samples) is performed by the same team without independent verification, which is a weak and potentially biased quality check for a paper whose core claim rests on annotation quality.

No discussion of potential copyright/IP or safety issues inherent to using a commercial diffusion model (FLUX) to generate large-scale training imagery (e.g., recognizable fictional objects/scenes such as the 'Throne' category resembling copyrighted media, or photorealistic depictions of people), which is a relevant ethical consideration for a dataset-release paper.

Related work framing somewhat overstates limitations of prior synthetic-data methods (e.g., dismissing teacher-bounded pseudo-labeling) without an empirical baseline using a strong modern teacher (e.g., SAM/SAM-HQ) trained/fine-tuned at comparable synthetic data scale, which would be needed to isolate the benefit of the proposed multi-modal diffusion-feature extraction versus simply more teacher-labeled synthetic data.

Dataset statistics show only 1,676 unique objects across 139,981 images, suggesting substantial redundancy/repetition within object categories that may inflate apparent dataset scale without proportionally increasing real diversity.

Writing quality has multiple typos, inconsistent method-name capitalization, and awkward phrasing (e.g., 'proving an importance of the data scale and and impact of overfitting'), suggesting the manuscript would benefit from a more careful revision pass.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (139,981 image) synthetic SOD dataset, substantially larger than existing manually annotated benchmarks (>2x combined), addressing a genuine data scarcity bottleneck in dichotomous/high-resolution SOD.

Novel multi-modal label extraction pipeline that fuses FLUX DiT intermediate features, concept attention maps, and DINO-v3 features to produce pixel-level masks directly from the generative process, avoiding reliance on an external teacher segmentation model and its performance ceiling.

Ambiguity-aware multi-mask decoder with multiple-choice-learning-style training and learned IoU-based branch selection is a sensible and lightweight way to model saliency ambiguity, and the architecture is simpler than many competing high-resolution SOD backbones (DPT + DINO-v3) while remaining competitive in parameter/FLOP count (Table 10).

Reasonably comprehensive empirical evaluation: cross-dataset generalization (Table 2), standard benchmark fine-tuning comparisons (Table 3), comparisons against other synthetic data generation methods (MaskFactory, DatasetDM) in Table 4, and ablations isolating iterative generation (Table 5), modality fusion (Table 6), backbone/mask-count choices (Table 7), and prompt generation strategy (Table 8/9).

Multi-stage quality filtering (consistency filtering, VLM-based mask/semantic validation) and quantitative image-quality comparisons (IS/FID vs MaskFactory and DatasetDM) add some rigor to the claim that the synthetic data is higher quality than prior synthetic SOD datasets.
Iterative, performance-feedback-driven category reweighting is a reasonable mechanism to adaptively focus generation on weak categories, and ablations show it helps (Table 5).
weaknesses: Core technical descriptions are underspecified in places: the exact mechanism by which DiT feature maps, concept attention maps, and DINO-v3 features are converted into a binary/soft ground-truth mask (the actual 'decoding' step performed during dataset construction vs. at test time) is not fully clear; the paper conflates the dataset-generation decoder with the final S3OD model architecture in Figure 2/Figure 3, hurting reproducibility of the labeling pipeline.

No large-scale human/manual annotation baseline or inter-annotator-agreement-style validation beyond a small internal spot-check (1,000 masks, 14 with minor issues) is provided to firmly establish mask quality at scale; reliance on a Gemma-3 VLM for quality filtering introduces another potentially biased judge without independent validation against human raters at scale.

Cross-dataset generalization claims (e.g., 50% MAE reduction) are compared against models trained on relatively small single real datasets (e.g., DIS-5K with 3,000 images) rather than stronger multi-dataset or larger-scale baselines, which may inflate the apparent advantage of scale rather than isolating the contribution of the proposed multi-modal label extraction method itself.

In Table 3, S3OD's non-oracle numbers are not uniformly best across all datasets/metrics (e.g., mixed results against BiRefNet/MVANet on HRSOD-TE and DUTS-TE), yet the oracle variant S3OD* (using ground truth to select the best of 3 masks, explicitly stated as incomparable to other methods) is prominently reported in the same table, risking a misleading impression of the real performance gain from the multi-mask architecture.

Limited discussion of failure modes or limitations of the synthetic pipeline (e.g., rare/compositional categories, fine boundary accuracy versus teacher-based HR-SOD methods, domain gap for non-object-centric scenes) and no discussion of ethical considerations around large-scale diffusion-generated training data (inherited biases, licensing/provenance of generated imagery).

Ablation studies (Tables 5-9) appear to use single runs on comparatively small subsets without variance/error bars or multiple seeds, making it difficult to assess the statistical significance of reported deltas (e.g., 3.6%/5.3% F-measure gains, 44.7% Inception Score increase).

The paper has some clarity/polish issues (minor typos, dense notation, some unclear sentences), and several important implementation details (fusion module architecture specifics, exact LLM used for prompting, full training hyperparameters) are deferred to a brief appendix rather than fully specified in the main text.

The efficiency comparison (Table 10) shows S3OD has lower FPS than MVANet and BiRefNet despite similar or lower FLOPs/parameters, and this discrepancy between theoretical efficiency and measured throughput is not discussed or explained.

strengths: Introduces a novel multi-modal diffusion-based data generation pipeline that jointly extracts FLUX DiT feature maps, concept-attention maps, and DINO-v3 features to decode high-quality masks directly from the generative process, avoiding the performance ceiling of relying on an external teacher segmentation model.

Produces a large-scale (139k image) high-resolution synthetic SOD dataset (S3OD) that is more than 2x the size of all existing SOD datasets combined, with a multi-stage quality-filtering pipeline (consistency, VLM-based mask quality, semantic validation) and demonstrated low synthetic-to-real domain gap via UMAP and precision/recall analysis against real distributions.
Proposes an iterative, feedback-driven generation framework that reweights category sampling based on per-category model performance, with ablations showing consistent gains across rounds.

Ambiguity-aware multi-mask decoder architecture is well-motivated, simple, and ablated (backbone choice, number of mask branches, auxiliary loss regularization/decay), addressing a genuine limitation of prior single-output SOD models.

Extensive empirical evaluation: cross-dataset generalization across six SOD/DIS benchmarks, fine-tuned SOTA comparisons, retraining of existing baselines (BiRefNet, MVANet) on S3OD to isolate dataset effect, comparison to other synthetic-data generation methods (MaskFactory, DatasetDM), zero-shot and fine-tuned transfer to camouflaged object detection, and comparisons with SAM-based pipelines and model efficiency (FLOPs/FPS).

Comprehensive appendix with feature-complementarity visualizations, prompt-generation analysis, dataset quality metrics (IS/FID), and thorough ablations, indicating good experimental rigor and transparency about limitations.
weaknesses: No held-out test split is released for S3OD (explicitly acknowledged), which limits its future use as a standardized benchmark and makes some internal evaluations (e.g., category feedback scoring) harder to verify independently.

The pipeline depends on several large proprietary/closed components (FLUX-Krea, GPT-4 for prompt generation, Gemma-3 VLM for filtering), which raises reproducibility concerns as these models evolve or become inaccessible, and makes exact replication costly.

Some reported gains (e.g., 'up to 50% error reduction') are best-case numbers from selected comparisons rather than consistent average improvements; the actual per-benchmark gains vary substantially (e.g., some DUT-OMRON or UHRSD improvements are much more modest), so headline claims may overstate typical performance.

The multi-mask decoder ablation (Table 15) shows only small numerical differences across configurations, and given the limited grid search (four hand-picked configurations due to compute cost), the robustness/significance of the specific λ_reg/γ choice is not strongly established.

The 'S3OD*' oracle (best-of-three-masks) evaluation, while appropriately caveated as not directly comparable, is still used to support the ambiguity-aware architecture narrative without a more rigorous multi-hypothesis evaluation metric (e.g., generalized energy distance) or human-annotated ambiguity ground truth.

Potential category/taxonomy overlap between the ImageNet-derived category set used for synthetic data generation and evaluation benchmark categories is not discussed, which could inflate apparent 'zero-shot generalization' claims (e.g., for COD transfer).

The paper's core novelty is largely a combination of existing techniques (diffusion feature extraction, concept-attention, DINO features, MHP-style multi-mask decoding, iterative curriculum sampling) rather than a fundamentally new method, which somewhat limits the conceptual contribution despite strong empirical execution.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (139K image) synthetic SOD dataset that is substantially larger than all existing DIS/HR-SOD datasets combined, generated via a novel multi-modal pipeline combining FLUX DiT feature maps, concept-attention maps, and DINO-v3 features for mask decoding directly from the generative process.

Extensive empirical evaluation spanning cross-dataset generalization (DIS↔SOD transfer), fine-tuned SOTA comparisons on DIS-5K and multiple HR-SOD benchmarks, zero-shot and fine-tuned transfer to camouflaged object detection (COD), and retraining other backbones (BiRefNet, MVANet) on S3OD to show the data itself (not just the proposed architecture) drives gains.

Reasonably thorough ablation studies covering the iterative generation feedback loop, individual vs. combined feature modalities, backbone choice, number of mask branches, and multi-mask decoder regularization hyperparameters.

Quantitative synthetic-data quality assessment (FID, Inception Score, UMAP domain coverage, precision/recall against real data manifold) and manual mask-quality verification, going beyond simply reporting downstream accuracy.

Ambiguity-aware multi-mask decoder with IoU-score-based test-time selection and a decaying auxiliary loss to prevent branch collapse is a sensible, lightweight adaptation of multiple-choice learning to the SOD ambiguity problem, simplifying architecture relative to recent SOTA pipelines (BiRefNet, MVANet).
weaknesses: The authors explicitly do not release/define a test split for S3OD, which limits reproducibility of the exact iterative-generation feedback mechanism and category-weighting results described in Section 4.2.

The data-generation pipeline depends on multiple large closed/proprietary models (FLUX-Krea, GPT-4 for prompting, Gemma-3 for filtering), raising reproducibility and cost concerns beyond what is addressed in the limitations section.

The paper repeatedly acknowledges that standard SOD/DIS/COD benchmarks are saturated (e.g., comparable performance across transformer backbones, small test sets like CAMO with 250 images), which undercuts the significance of several "state-of-the-art" claims even as the paper leans heavily on them.

Core architectural components (DPT backbone, multiple-choice/MCL-style multi-mask prediction, focal+IoU loss) are largely adopted from prior work; the primary novelty is concentrated in the data pipeline, yet the paper frames the overall contribution as both architectural and data-centric, which slightly overstates architectural novelty.

Comparisons between models trained on S3OD (139K images) and baselines trained on much smaller real datasets conflate the effect of raw data scale with the proposed multi-modal extraction method; the dataset-generation-method ablation (Table 5, MaskFactory/DatasetDM comparisons) is done on a subsampled, size-matched subset, which somewhat mitigates but does not fully resolve this confound across the rest of the paper's main tables.

The oracle-style S3ODNet* metric (best match among 3 predicted masks vs. ground truth) is reported in the same SOTA comparison table (Table 4) as standard single-prediction methods, which could create a misleading impression of the method's real deployed performance despite the caveat in text.

Generalization claims ("unify DIS and HR-SOD," strong transfer to COD) are somewhat overstated given that DIS, HR-SOD, and COD are all closely related binary foreground segmentation tasks; broader generalization to substantially different dense-prediction tasks is not demonstrated.

Limited discussion of potential biases introduced by the diffusion-generated dataset (e.g., ImageNet-taxonomy category coverage, demographic/scene biases inherited from FLUX) and no broader ethical discussion beyond a brief limitations paragraph.

Minor clarity issues: inconsistent notation/typos (e.g., dataset name rendering, mixed use of "S3OD"/"S30D"), and some ablations (e.g., Table 9) mix backbone and branch-count variables, making isolation of individual design choices harder to interpret precisely.

strengths: Introduces a large-scale (139K+ image) synthetic dataset for salient object segmentation generated via a novel multi-modal diffusion pipeline that combines FLUX DiT feature maps, concept-attention maps, and DINO-v3 features, providing an interesting alternative to teacher-model pseudo-labeling or mask-conditioned generation approaches.

Proposes an ambiguity-aware multi-mask decoder with a principled auxiliary loss (relaxed/decaying regularization) to avoid branch collapse, with a careful ablation (Table 15) justifying design choices.

Extensive and convincing empirical evaluation: cross-dataset generalization across six SOD benchmarks, fine-tuned SOTA comparisons on DIS/HR-SOD, zero-shot and fine-tuned transfer to camouflaged object detection (COD10K/CAMO/NC4K), comparisons against other synthetic-data generation baselines (MaskFactory, DatasetDM), and comparisons with SAM-based methods.

Thorough ablation studies covering iterative generation rounds, modality contributions (DINO-v3/DiT/concept maps), backbone choice, number of mask branches, and LLM-based prompt diversity, which support the paper's central claims.

Good appendix material including domain-gap analysis (UMAP, precision/recall vs. real data manifold), feature complementarity visualizations, model efficiency comparison (FLOPs/params/FPS), and transparent discussion of limitations (no synthetic test split, residual mask artifacts, compute cost).
The iterative, feedback-driven data generation framework that reweights categories based on model weaknesses is a sensible and relatively novel idea for scaling synthetic datasets efficiently.
weaknesses: Heavy reliance on a large proprietary/closed diffusion model (FLUX, 12B params) and its specific internal feature extraction (DiT block layers, concept-attention) raises reproducibility concerns, since results and the pipeline are tightly coupled to this exact model/checkpoint (FLUX-Krea) and may not transfer to other generators.

The multi-stage quality filtering (consistency filtering, Gemma-3 VLM mask/semantic validation) involves several hand-tuned thresholds (τ=0.8, ≤5 components, >70% coverage) whose sensitivity is not studied, and reliance on another generative/VLM model to judge quality could introduce circular biases that are not fully analyzed.

No human study or crowd-sourced quality/diversity assessment of the synthetic dataset beyond automated metrics (Inception Score, FID, CLIP score), which may not fully capture label correctness or semantic diversity meaningful to downstream SOD tasks.

Some of the headline cross-dataset generalization gains partially stem from comparisons against models trained on much smaller real datasets (e.g., 3,000–5,000 images) vs. 139K synthetic images; a more controlled comparison equalizing data scale (beyond the 10K-subsample ablation) would better isolate the contribution of the generation method itself versus sheer data scale.

The paper acknowledges but does not deeply address that several HR-SOD benchmarks (UHRSD, DAVIS-S) are already near-saturated, so improvements there are marginal, and the paper's strongest claims rest primarily on DUT-OMRON and DIS, somewhat narrowing the practical significance of the generalization claims.

Dataset generation and training pipeline is computationally expensive (8×H200 GPUs for 2 days for training, plus the cost of generating 139K high-resolution diffusion samples across 3 rounds), which could limit accessibility/reproducibility for other researchers despite the paper's claim that generation is 'orders of magnitude faster' than manual labeling.
No public release statement (code/dataset availability) is clearly confirmed in the main text, which is important given the paper's central contribution is the dataset itself.
